questions.q: What does Databricks SQL run on top of, and what is its syntax heritage?
options: Apache Spark, with syntax tracing back through Spark SQL to Hive SQL
A fork of PostgreSQL
A proprietary engine with no relation to any other SQL dialect
Microsoft SQL Server's engine, licensed for cloud use
questions.explain: Databricks SQL runs on Apache Spark, and its syntax heritage traces through Spark SQL back to Hive SQL.

questions.q: How does Databricks SQL quote identifiers, and which other dialect in this course shares that convention?
options: Backticks — the same convention MySQL uses
Square brackets — the same convention T-SQL uses
Double quotes — the same convention PostgreSQL uses
Databricks SQL does not support quoted identifiers
questions.explain: Databricks SQL quotes identifiers with backticks, identical to MySQL's convention, rather than T-SQL's brackets or ANSI double quotes.

questions.q: What table format typically backs Databricks SQL tables?
options: Delta Lake, an open table format adding transactional guarantees and versioning over cloud storage files
A proprietary binary format unique to Databricks with no public specification
Plain CSV files with no transactional guarantees
The same row/page storage engine T-SQL uses
questions.explain: Databricks SQL tables are usually backed by Delta Lake, which adds transactional guarantees and versioning on top of files in cloud storage.

questions.q: What does LATERAL VIEW explode() do in Databricks SQL / Spark SQL?
options: Turns each element of an array or map column into its own output row, paired with the parent row's other columns
Deletes duplicate rows from a result set
Casts a column to a different data type
Combines two tables using a full outer join
questions.explain: LATERAL VIEW explode() expands an array or map column so each element becomes its own row, conceptually similar to what CROSS APPLY does in T-SQL but with very different syntax.

questions.q: How does LATERAL VIEW explode() compare conceptually to T-SQL's CROSS APPLY?
options: Conceptually similar — both expand a correlated value per source row — but the syntax is very different
They are unrelated concepts that happen to share no similarity
They are byte-for-byte identical syntax
CROSS APPLY is the exact SQL Server name for LATERAL VIEW explode()
questions.explain: Both achieve a similar end result — producing one row per element of a correlated set — but LATERAL VIEW explode() is a Spark-specific keyword combination, not a JOIN-family keyword like CROSS APPLY.
